extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive rules about how positive laws and institutions should be designed to conform to the fundamental principle of each regime (democracy, aristocracy, monarchy, despotism), including remedies to regime-specific vices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve frugality and equality of fortunes in democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws must maintain frugality because frugality sustains equality of fortunes; each is both cause and effect and one cannot subsist without the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation should favor habits of economy, moderation and limit excesses that create inequality; if equality of fortunes decays, the democracy itself follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor commerce but prevent wealth excesses in commercial democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: When democracy is founded on commerce, commerce produces frugality and useful moeurs, but an excess of riches will destroy the spirit of commerce and produce inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws should promote commerce (which brings moderation, work, order) while instituting measures (see inheritance and redistribution measures) to prevent extreme accumulation that undermines civic virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide fortunes as commerce grows (progressive redistribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws, by their dispositions, should divide fortunes as commerce enlarges them, putting poor citizens in comfortable conditions to work and keeping rich citizens moderate so they must work to keep or acquire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use legal mechanisms to ensure wealth created by commerce does not concentrate—policies to redistribute or limit accumulations in proportion to commercial growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal inheritance in commercial republics
rubrics_metrics.description: A very good law in a commercial republic is that which gives all children an equal portion in their father's succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equal division of inheritance prevents children from being richer than parents and promotes avoidance of luxury and encouragement of work; applies particularly to commercial republics (not necessarily to non-commercial states).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit dowries and private wealth transmission (family-law limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appropriate (notably non-commercial republics), the legislator should put strict limits on dowries and transfers to prevent luxury and corruption of moeurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family-law restrictions reduce concentration of wealth and curb social excesses; the marginal note: 'On y doit borner beaucoup les dots des femmes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ a fixed senatorial body as moral exemplar
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a permanent body (senate) whose age, virtue and gravity confer entry; such senators, shown before the people as simulacra of gods, inspire sentiments carried into families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fixed senate attached to ancient institutions will anchor customs and moeurs; it should act as the rule of manners and be made for life when its role is to be the perpetual model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attach the senate to ancient institutions and customs
rubrics_metrics.description: The senate must adhere to old institutions and ensure people and magistrates never depart from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserving customs and ancient maxims is generally restorative of virtue; new institutions are usually the source of abuses and old institutions serve as corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make senatorial tenure life-long when senate serves as moral deposit
rubrics_metrics.description: In a senate intended to be the rule and repository of moeurs, senators should be elected for life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare practice at Rome and Lacedaemon; short-term bodies that prepare business are different and may change periodically, but permanent moral guardians should have life tenure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish censors or magistrates to oversee moeurs
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be censors with eyes on the people and the senate to restore corrupted moeurs, note tepidity, judge negligence and correct faults as laws punish crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Censors must be empowered to rectify moral decay; public institutions of supervision (e.g., Roman censors, Lacedaemonian guardians) are essential to maintain civic virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public accusation for certain moral offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Public accusation (e.g., of adultery) is an admirable law to maintain purity of moeurs because it intimidates and deters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making certain accusations public operates as a deterrent to immorality; employ with caution given liberty costs and differing social contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote extreme subordination of youth to elders and citizens to magistrates
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing maintains moeurs more than extreme subordination of young to old and citizens to magistrates; respect for elders and authority restrains both groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws should foster deference and strict obedience norms where republican moeurs require strong civic self-restraint; examples: Lacedaemon practice of obedience to magistrates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplement weak republican coercion with paternal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: In a republic there is not the same repressing force as in other governments; laws should supplement this by reinforcing paternal authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting parents stronger powers over children (property, discipline) helps maintain public moeurs when state coercion is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make laws in aristocracies that foster moderation and reduce inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Because aristocracies tend toward great inequality, laws should aim to foster an 'spirit of moderation' (the virtue of aristocracy) and restore, as far as possible, equality that the constitution removes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation should equalize fortunes among nobles and between nobles and people where feasible, curb privileges that produce hatred and jealousy, and use institutional checks to prevent abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require nobles to display modesty and simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Fame and splendor of nobles should be tempered by modesty and manners; when nobles are indistinguishable from the people in dress and pleasures, the people forget their weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws and customs should discourage ostentation among nobles and encourage social proximity to the populace to preserve social cohesion and reduce resentment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attach privileges to the corporate body, not individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Privileges must belong to the senate/corporate body and not be personal prerogatives that change the nature of aristocracy into monarchy-like personal rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid personal prerogatives for nobles that create distinct classes of special rights; respect for the senate as an institution suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent nobles from exploiting tax collection and public revenues
rubrics_metrics.description: Nobles must not levy tributes or appropriate public revenues; when they do, they become despotic agents who ruin the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign tax collection away from nobles, tax the privileged classes as others, and require transparency in public revenues (display of treasures) to make people feel they share ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbid noble participation in commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws should forbid nobles from engaging in commerce to prevent monopolies and excessive wealth accumulation among the aristocracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Venice's law preventing noble commerce is cited; commerce should remain the profession of equals to avoid nobles becoming merchants and creating abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide strong magistratures to check noble arrogance
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristocracies need strong, sometimes severe magistratures (e.g., ephors, inquisitors) to mortify pride of domination and to keep nobles in line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create offices capable of terrifying nobles when necessary, without formal constraints that would neutralize their effect; but balance to avoid sliding into tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating permanent mechanisms that perpetuate noble wealth (primogeniture, majorats, substitutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws should remove the right of primogeniture and forbid substitutions, retraits lignagers, majorats and adoptions that perpetuate family grandeur in aristocracies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuous partition of inheritances keeps noble fortunes from growing exorbitant; mechanisms used in monarchies to perpetuate families are inappropriate in aristocracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve noble disputes quickly and use arbitration
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws should ensure that disputes among nobles are promptly decided to prevent private quarrels becoming family feuds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use arbitrators or fast procedures to avoid litigations that enlarge into social conflicts between noble families.

rubrics_metrics.name: In monarchies, fashion laws to sustain honor and hereditary nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: Because honor is the principle of monarchy, laws must sustain that honor, make nobility hereditary (as a bond between prince and people), and allow substitutions/retrait lignager appropriate to monarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept legal mechanisms that tie dignity to fiefs and permit leaving most property to a single child (primogeniture) insofar as it supports the monarchical principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor commerce within the limits of monarchical constitution and order taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws should encourage all commerce that the monarchical constitution can bear, and impose order on tax levying so it is not heavier than burdens can bear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote commerce for state's needs (court expenditures) but ensure tax systems are fair and not excessively burdensome, since overburdening produces fatigue and then idleness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper executive promptitude with legal slowness in monarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: Monarchies benefit from prompt execution but need laws to introduce a degree of slowness to prevent reckless rapidity by a single ruler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bodies that deliberate slowly (councils, legislative bodies) provide reflection absent from the monarch's immediate will; use procedural delay to check unwise haste.

rubrics_metrics.name: In despotism, limit laws to a few fixed principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Despotism's principle is fear; in such states few laws are needed—two or three ideas suffice—and new laws are unnecessary and dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep laws minimal and consistent with the prince's absolute power; do not introduce many legal complexities which despotism neither requires nor safely tolerates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve some customs to moderate princely avarice (succession taxes/customs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the prince seizes successions and property, customary limits (e.g., small succession take) can moderate his greed and prevent total precarity of property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ottoman practice of taking a modest percentage on successions; such customs provide some stability of property and avoid total abandonment of agriculture and industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix succession by fundamental law to avoid revolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear, visible rule of succession (birth order) that strikes the eye is best; when succession is arbitrary, it causes many revolutions and makes the throne precarious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enshrine hereditary succession rules as fundamental law to prevent princes from choosing successors arbitrarily and to reduce fratricidal struggles common in despotic and elective-in-practice principalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid abolishing property rights wholesale in despotisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws that deprive people of land ownership and hereditary succession result in decline of agriculture, ruin industry, and cause desolation and desertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect some property rights or customs; complete appropriation by prince destroys incentives to improve land and invest in long-term works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use religion and social institutions where they reinforce the regime's principle
rubrics_metrics.description: In despotic states religion often adds to fear and can be used to reinforce obedience; laws should account for the social role of religion in supporting political order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the strength of religious institutions in certain societies serves to buttress political power and may substitute for other legal mechanisms; craft laws accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design laws to remedy regime-specific abuses while supporting regime principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws should both favor the natural character of each constitution and remedy the abuses that result from that constitution's nature (e.g., slow councils to check monarchical haste, strong magistratures to check aristocratic pride).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators must tailor legal institutions to balance the advantages and counteract the predictable vices of each form of government; this is the core methodological principle throughout the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage institutions that reveal and make people 'share' public wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: If revenues are not distributed, show them to the people (triumphal processions, public treasuries) to make the populace feel they partake of the state's wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public display of state wealth can substitute for distribution in aristocratic regimes to maintain popular attachment to the order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid asylum or legal protections that obstruct law enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Any sort of asylum that prevents execution of laws undermines aristocracy and leads toward tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation should minimize extrajudicial safe-havens which allow subjects to evade legal accountability and thereby corrode the rule of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure accountability of magistrates except where independence is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates should be accountable for their conduct, but certain offices (e.g., censors) must have independence during their term to exercise moral oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow reviews and accounts for magistrates generally, yet preserve immunity or independence for offices tasked with censorial or moral roles to prevent their neutralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use demographic/cultural differences to adapt legal ages and minority rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Age of majority and minority rules should consider climate and local customs (e.g., earlier majority in warm climates where people marry young).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation must be sensitive to local social realities—e.g., if majority begins at 15 in some societies, legal structures (minority length) should reflect that.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit cessions and bankrupt relief in moderate regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Cession of goods and certain insolvency measures are natural in moderate governments and republics because of higher confidence in citizens' probity and the need to temper private ruin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt humane bankruptcy rules that avoid ignominious punishment and excessive imprisonment to prevent civil discord (as exemplified by Roman law reforms).
